---
title: Names and numbers from evidence
description: Every number, identifier and name in the final answer must appear in a tool result the run really read. If one does not, the model typed it rather than read it — a deterministic check, no second model.
---

> A storage engineer asks which array port is affected. The agent answers with a
> port row: alias `SHPMAXDLVAP001-FA0`, FCID `0xef0101`. Both look exactly like
> the real thing. Neither appears in **any** tool result from that turn — the
> model typed them. That is a real answer from a real production run, and
> nothing in the conversation could have caught it. The framework watched every
> tool result land, so it can.

`.namesAndNumbersFromEvidence()` requires every **number, identifier and name**
in the final answer to appear in a tool result the run actually read.

```ts
const agent = Agent.create({ provider, model })
  .tool(showInterfaceStatus)
  .tool(showFlogi)
  .namesAndNumbersFromEvidence({ posture: 'guard' })
  .build();

const answer = await agent.run({ message: 'which array port is affected?' });
```

## What it is — and what it provably is not

It is a **fabrication detector, not a correctness judge.**

It catches invented values. It **cannot** catch a false claim assembled from
real values: *"fc1/3 is healthy"* when the data says the port is down uses
entirely grounded tokens — `fc1/3` is in the evidence, "healthy" is a word — and
the check passes it without a murmur. So does *"the outage started at 08:15"*
when 08:15 is a timestamp belonging to a different port. If you read this as a
hallucination check you will trust it for the one thing it cannot do.

It cannot catch **mis-referral** either — an answer whose every sentence is true
*of the wrong thing*. The gate judges values against evidence, so *"that machine
has no backup record"* passes with every value grounded even when the machine
the sentence is about was never the one you asked about. That is a recorded
failure: a model resolved "that machine" out of its own earlier answer, called
the lookup tool with a truncated job name, and got a genuine "nothing found"
back — which the gate then grounded, correctly, in a genuine tool result. The
referent was bound wrong one seam earlier, at the **argument**, and that is the
defect [Context Integrity](doc:context-integrity)'s choice-seam check owns
(`unsupported-argument`, armed by `argumentsFrom` on the tool). By the time an
answer exists the wrong lookup has already been served as evidence, so this
check is not the place it could ever be caught.

It is also conservative in the other direction. Small numbers, all-letters names
and quantities with units (`32G`, `47 flaps`, `892 CRC errors`) are not
examined, because a **false accusation costs a real turn** — and on a weak model
a false accusation triggers exactly the retry loop this library exists to
remove. A missed fabrication is a miss; a refused good answer is damage.

## Why it is deterministic

No second model, no embedding, no LLM judge. The check is set membership over
normalized tokens: it costs microseconds and answers identically on every run.

That constraint is the point. This library's thesis is that structure lets a
smaller model perform like a bigger one — so a guard that needed a *bigger*
model to police the small one would invert the whole value proposition, and
would fail precisely where the small model is deployed: offline, cheap, fast.

## The three postures

Same three words as [`.skillGraph({ strictness })`](doc:skill-graph-quickstart)
and a **separate** option, because routing authority and evidence discipline are
different decisions.

| `posture` | What happens |
|---|---|
| `'assist'` *(default)* | Record and flag. The answer goes out unchanged — you learn how often it happens before you act on it. |
| `'guard'` | The unsupported values are named back to the model, which gets **one** more ordinary turn. Survivors ship flagged. **Recommended for weaker models.** |
| `'rails'` | The same one revision, then `run()` raises `UnsupportedValuesError` rather than return an answer that still carries them. |

`guard` is a branch of the ReAct loop, not a special mode: the correction is one
more ordinary turn, with its own `iteration_start` / `llm_start` bracket and its
own `cost.tick` — and the tools are still on the wire, so the model can go and
*fetch* the value it guessed at. One revision per turn, latched: a model that
cannot ground a value on its second try will not on its fifth. The one
exception is an ENFORCING answer validation (below): there the answer may yet
be withheld, so the revision and every later call of the run are served no
tools and dispatch none, and a tool that writes or sends never runs twice.

```ts
// guard, in the run's own record:
// route_decided { chosen: 'evidence-recheck' }
// evidence_checked { action: 'revision-asked', unsupported: [ … ] }
// route_decided { chosen: 'final' }
// evidence_checked { action: 'grounded', afterRevision: true }   ← it worked
```

**To withhold rather than flag** a typed answer, list the gate in an enforcing
answer validation: `.answerValidation({ …, agentChecks: ['names-and-numbers'] })`.
The posture still decides whether the model gets its one repair turn, which is
served no tools while the validation enforces: the library cannot tell a tool
that only reads from one that writes, so a repair can never repeat a refund or
a send before the answer is withheld. Whatever survives it fails the
validation, so the answer is withheld and no draft token of it is streamed. See
[Let the agent's own checks hold the answer](doc:output-schema) on the output
schema page.

## What counts as evidence

* **Tool results** — the `role: 'tool'` turns of the conversation. That is the
  whole corpus. Results that are JSON are walked **structurally** (every key,
  every leaf) rather than searched as text, so a value that merely appears
  inside an unrelated field does not read as grounded.
* **Tool call arguments do not count.** The model typed those; grounding a value
  because the model passed it to a tool would let any invention launder itself
  through one failed lookup.
* **The model's own earlier answers do not count**, for the same reason.

Values the **user** supplied are exempt without being declared: this turn's
message, the conversation's user and system turns, and the composed system
prompt (base prompt, skill bodies, retrieved passages). The user gave them, so
they were not invented.

Spelling differences are normalised on both sides, which is where a naive
implementation produces its worst false positives: `41,200` in prose matches the
JSON number `41200`, `2048.0` matches `2048`, and `0xef0101` matches `ef0101`.

## Show the script the answer was computed with

A data agent often hands the script it ran back in the answer, because the app
says "always show the script". Read as prose, the script's constants and format
specifications (`{mean:.2f}`) become values to ground — and the cheapest
revision that passes the check is to delete the script.

Two opt-ins fix that, and both rest on one declaration: a tool that runs a
program says so (`script: { argument: 'code', language }` on `defineTool`;
`codeRunnerTool` declares it). Each call of such a tool records the program it
was handed and what its runner reported.

* **`.scriptTravelsWithTheAnswer()`** — the library attaches the recorded
  program itself, under the answer, labelled from the run record. The model
  never retypes it, so there is nothing to check. A prose answer gets it as text
  after the `---` separator; every answer gets it as data on
  `turn_end.scripts`; a typed answer gets the data only.
* **`code: 'match'`** — a fenced block the model wrote anyway is compared, byte
  for byte after removing only the Markdown wrapper, with the programs this
  turn's calls submitted. A match is script content: it yields no values to
  check and is labelled with that call's outcome. Anything else stays prose,
  checked as before, labelled `unmatched`.

<CodeFile path="examples/features/120-script-artifact.ts" region="script-artifact" title="The script travels with the answer (local runner, mock model)" />

The label says only what the record proves:

| Label | Means |
|---|---|
| `completed, exit 0` | the runner reported exit code 0 |
| `completed with failure, exit 7` | the runner reported that non-zero exit code |
| `runner reported success; no exit code` | a bare verdict, no exit code — not proof the program ran to an exit |
| `runner reported failure; no exit code` | the same, for failure (a stopped process included) |
| `outcome unknown` | a timeout, a cancellation or an error with no runner facts, or a service error with no exit code |
| `tool call returned; execution not confirmed` | the tool returned, and no runner said how the program ended |
| `submitted` | the call never reached the tool (refused, never dispatched, or still open) |

What the record holds, by type:

* A tool declares its program argument with a `ToolScript`
  (`{ argument, language? }`). The argument must be a declared string property.
* Each call of a declaring tool files one `ScriptRow` on the findings ledger:
  the program the tool was handed, its UTF-8 `bytes` and `lines`, its
  `ScriptLabel`, and `exitCode` only when the runner gave one. A row belongs to
  a `dispatch`: the call's order within the turn. A provider that reuses a call
  id still makes two calls, and a pause and its resume are one.
* `evidence_checked.scripts` is a `ScriptsVerdict`, with one
  `ScriptBlockVerdict` per fenced block. Each verdict holds either the matched
  call with its label, or `unmatched` with an `UnmatchedReason`:
  `no-submission-this-turn`, `over-size`, or `kept-out`. Only a reader of a
  redacted record produces `kept-out`; a live run never does.
* `turn_end.scripts` is a `TurnEndScripts`: one `ShownScript` per attached
  program, plus how many were left out. `closedFence` says the library closed a
  fence the text above left open before attaching; `withheldFromText` says the
  programs are in the data only (see the gotchas).
* `.scriptTravelsWithTheAnswer()` takes `ScriptTravelOptions`. `which` is
  `'last'` (the default) or `'all'`; `maxBytes` defaults to 4,000.
* The answer that stands files one `ScriptShownRow` per block, for the
  standing record.

Gotchas:

* **Code is never evidence.** A matched script grounds nothing: a value in the
  prose that also sits in the script still needs a tool result, and a script
  that printed `99999` proves it printed `99999`, not that revenue was `99999`.
* **Nothing is normalized.** A copy that differs by one byte — a trailing space,
  CRLF for LF, a combining accent — is a different program, so it is a miss.
* **Formatting exempts nothing.** Inline code, indented code, a fence with
  leading spaces and a fence that never closes are prose.
* **A block ends where a renderer ends it.** A block closes at a fence of its
  own character at least as long as its opening, indented by up to three
  spaces, as in CommonMark. Text after that point is prose, even if the
  program submitted to the tool went on.
* **Reading stops where a renderer could disagree.** From these lines on, no
  block is read:
  - a fence indented inside a list;
  - an HTML block;
  - a `$$` math line;
  - a closing fence with a trailing tab;
  - a block whose program holds a fence run as long as its own fence.
  Everything after the stop is checked as prose. To show a program that holds
  three backticks, use a longer fence, as the attached copy always does.
* **Only this turn.** A block is compared with this turn's calls only; a
  program from an earlier turn is a miss.
* **Bounded.** A program over 32,768 UTF-8 bytes keeps its facts but no text
  (never matched, never attached); 16 calls a turn keep a row; 32 blocks an
  answer are read; an attached program over `maxBytes` (default 4,000 bytes) is
  cut and says it is incomplete.
* **The attachment never renders inside an unfinished block.** If the answer
  ends inside a fence the model never closed, the library closes it before the
  attached program. If the answer holds a line after which a renderer could pair
  fences another way (an indented fence, raw HTML, `$$`), the text names each
  script and says it is not shown here; the program rides `turn_end.scripts`.
* **Names and ids are shown as code.** A tool's name and a call id appear as
  inline code, with line breaks and invisible characters written as escapes:
  a provider's id can never start a paragraph of its own.
* **The record attests the exact call.** The program on a row is the one read
  just before the tool ran; a tool that edits its arguments afterwards does not
  change it. A runner's exit code reaches only the call that ran the program,
  even when two agents share one tool and their providers reuse an id.
* **A redaction policy** keeps the program out of every record; the label and
  the counts stay. The attached text is part of the answer `run()` returns,
  which no policy covers — an app that attaches scripts shows what its own tool
  was handed.

## Round a plain decimal without inventing evidence

Use `decimalRounding: true` when an answer should report a carried measurement
at fewer decimal places. It is off by default, so existing applications keep
exact matching. With it on, plain decimals become checked data even below
`minDigits`: `5.203` can ground `5.20` or `5.2`, but not `5.3`. The answer's
written precision matters: `5.249` can ground `5.2`, but not `5.20`.
Original normalized decimal spellings are compared exactly: a source of `1`
does not justify invented low-order digits such as `1.000000000001`. Source
spellings above 256 characters are not eligible for rounding.

<CodeFile path="examples/features/103-evidence-rounding-ranges.ts" region="numeric-evidence" title="Decimal rounding and numeric ranges (mock only)" />

The evidence event reports the accepted rounding under `computed`, with
`derivation: 'rounded'` and `from` naming the carried value and its result
location. Exact evidence wins first. This option only rounds one carried
number; it adds no unitless sums, ratios, differences or unit conversions.
Whole numbers still need an exact match if they are checked, and identifiers
never round. Declare a shape when a numeric spelling is an ID in your app: a carried source
matching that shape is excluded from rounding too, even when a rounded
spelling would no longer match it.
The existing `figures: true` option separately enables measurement units and
its established arithmetic checks.

The same number in scientific notation counts too. Scripts often print small
values as `1.12e-02`. With `decimalRounding: true`, such a token in a tool's
text output is read as the exact decimal it states, so an answer's `0.0112` is
grounded, `0.011` is recorded as a rounding, and `0.012` or `1.12` is still
flagged. An answer written in scientific notation (`1.12e-2`) is checked at
the precision it was written with. A value with no fractional places after
expansion matches digit for digit: `1.2e+21` grounds `1200000000000000000000`.
Only a whole token counts, so hashes and versions such as `9f3e10ab` or
`1.2e3-rc` stay identifiers, and a percentage (`1.12%`) is never read as the
fraction `0.0112`.

## Check a range endpoint by endpoint

A range of exactly two plain numbers, separated by a hyphen or en dash, is
checked as two values only when the intact token was not returned by a tool.
An exact whole-token match wins first: a carried ZIP+4 `12345-6789`, part
number `1020-3040` or rack `10-20` remains one grounded identifier. Otherwise,
`1000–9000` checks `1000` and `9000` independently;
if a result carries only `1000`, only `9000` is flagged. `2-9ms` and
`2–9 ms` apply the trailing unit to both endpoints under `figures: true`.
The trailing unit must be one of the measurement units recognized by figures
(`%`, byte sizes, IOPS, throughput, `ms`, `us`, optionally `/s`). Signed
endpoints and decimals are supported; no interval arithmetic is inferred.

**Short bare endpoints are still prose.** At the default `minDigits: 4`,
an uncarried `0-13` is split but neither endpoint is checked. Use `minDigits: 1`
if both short counts must be verified. Opt-in decimal rounding and measurement figures
keep their own rules. This is token evidence, not proof that a range is ordered
correctly or that every number inside it was observed.

Dates, clock ranges, dotted versions and multipart IDs, such as
`2026-10-19`, `10:00-10:10`, `1.2.3-4` and `1-2-3`, are not numeric ranges.
App-declared identifier shapes are checked first: a shape matching `1-13`
keeps the token intact as your ID.

## Teaching it your identifiers

The default extractor guesses from digits and punctuation. It cannot know that
`ORD-4471` is an order number or that a WWN is a WWN. Declare the shapes and
they are checked by name — `shapes` composes with the defaults rather than
replacing them, and `exempt` removes what you know is safe.

```ts
.namesAndNumbersFromEvidence({
  posture: 'guard',
  shapes: [
    { name: 'wwn', match: /(?:[0-9a-f]{2}:){7}[0-9a-f]{2}/ },
    { name: 'order', match: /ord-\d{4,}/ },
  ],
  exempt: ['v9.35.0', /^build-\d+$/],
  minDigits: 4,   // when a BARE number stops being prose. Default 4.
})
```

A `NamesAndNumbersOptions` bag: `posture` (`EvidencePosture`), `shapes`
(`EvidenceShape[]` — each a `name` plus a `match` pattern, anchored to a whole
token), `exempt`, `minDigits`, `nudge`, `figures`, `decimalRounding`, and `recoveryInstruction`.

Since 9.96.0, `recoveryInstruction` accepts the exported
`EvidenceRecoveryInstruction` type: a string or synchronous callback returning
a string or `undefined`. The callback receives an exported
`EvidenceRecoveryContext`, a detached, frozen snapshot of the original request,
rejected draft, unsupported values, iteration, and available staged refs and
spender tools. Custom guidance is limited to 4,000 UTF-16 code units; invalid or
asynchronous returns fail rather than being silently ignored. For example, ask
the model to clarify missing dates or scope without suggesting invented values.
The framework appends this guidance to its fixed recovery frame in the next
request's system prompt, without adding synthetic conversation turns. The
lexical checker and single-revision budget remain unchanged: this does not prove
question interpretation or claim semantics, and does not suppress streamed draft
tokens.

## The staged-refs nudge

A recorded failure, and the reason this dial has a second half: four tool
results carried real numbers, a compute tool that could sum them was
registered, and the app's own prompt said to use it — yet the model summed the
numbers in its head and stated the total. The gate recorded *"appears in no
tool result"* and the answer shipped, because the posture only observed. The
instruction sat at the **top** of a long context; the numbers sat at the
**bottom**. Recency won.

`nudge: true` puts the instruction where recency works *for* it. When an
iteration's context holds a tool result staged by reference (an
[`artifacts.placement`](doc:artifacts) ticket) **and** a tool the model can
currently call declares [`wants`](doc:artifacts) over that ticket's kind, the
library appends **one** short line at the very end of that request:

```text
[staged data — this turn's tool results include data staged by reference:
'art_h7Kq…' (dataset/rows). Any derived number — a total, a sum, a difference,
an average — must come from a tool result, not from your own arithmetic. To
compute over the staged data, pass the ref string to `compute` and report what
it returns.]
```

Everything in it is composed from **declarations** — the ref and kind from the
placement mint (`Tool.resultKind`), the spender from `Tool.wants`, matched by
the same exact-string law dispatch uses, never by tool name. There is no prose
surface to write. The line is request-only (it never enters the conversation
history) and recomposed per iteration, so it exists exactly while both
conditions hold; each firing lands as `agentfootprint.agent.grounding_nudged`
with the refs and tools as data.

```ts
.namesAndNumbersFromEvidence({ posture: 'guard', nudge: true })
```

The nudge is advisory — the postures stay the guarantee. And under `guard` /
`rails` the two meet: when the flagged turn holds staged refs a served spender
can consume, the correction itself names them (*"pass 'art_h7Kq…'
(dataset/rows) to `compute` — compute the number there and answer with what it
returns"*), so the revision is handed the route, not just the demand. That
clause appears whenever a `wants` tool exists, with or without `nudge`.

## Reading the record

Every judgement fires `agentfootprint.agent.evidence_checked` — whatever the
posture and whatever the outcome, so a debugger can show the answer, the values
and whether the revision fixed them.

```ts
agent.on('agentfootprint.agent.evidence_checked', (e) => {
  // action: 'grounded' | 'revision-asked' | 'flagged' | 'refused'
  log.info({ action: e.payload.action, values: e.payload.unsupported });
});
```

`candidates` counts every value the check found in the answer; `lookedUp`
counts the ones it actually looked up in the tool results. The difference is
the values your user's message, the conversation or your own instructions
already held — those are never looked up, so a report says "looked up
`lookedUp` values", never `candidates`. A recording made before `lookedUp`
existed does not carry it.

After the run, `agent.unsupportedValues()` returns the terminal verdict — the
flagged `UnsupportedValue[]`, whether a revision was spent (`revised`), and
whether the answer was withheld (`refused`) — or `undefined` when every value
was grounded.

Under `'rails'` the run raises `UnsupportedValuesError` (an
`UnsupportedValuesContext`: the values, the candidate count, `revised`). The
error names the values and says what would satisfy the check; the refused
*answer* is not carried on it and stays in the commit log under whatever
redaction the run configured.

```ts
try {
  await agent.run({ message: 'which array port is affected?' });
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof UnsupportedValuesError) {
    log.warn({ invented: e.values.map((v) => v.value) });
  } else throw e;
}
```

The correction the loop sends is an authored frame followed by the quoted
values; `EVIDENCE_CHECK_FRAME_PREFIX` is exported so a transcript reader (or a
test) can recognise it without matching on prose.

## Composition

* With [`.outputSchema()`](doc:output-schema): the schema is judged **first** —
  an answer with the wrong shape is about to be replaced wholesale, so grounding
  it would pay for the same turn twice. The evidence gate judges what the schema
  let stand, and an answer that exhausted its schema retries is not judged at
  all. A typed answer is read value by value, the way a JSON tool result is:
  `{"counts":[1200,9750]}` checks `1200` and `9750`, never the text `1200,9750`.
  Its keys are your schema's field names, not values the model asserts, so a
  name like `p95LatencyMs` or `sha256` is never flagged. The price: an answer
  keyed by data (an order id as a key) is not checked on its keys — keep such
  ids in values.
* With `.answerValidation({ agentChecks: ['names-and-numbers'] })`: the gate is
  asked again of the exact JSON that validation delivers, after any output
  transform, and its verdict becomes a row of that report. A value no tool
  result carried fails it; a clean pass is `not-applicable`, because finding a
  value clears an answer without verifying it. The gate reads the first 20,000
  words and numbers of an answer; an answer longer than that makes the row
  `unreachable`, with the reason naming how many more were never looked up.
* With [`.reliability()`](doc:reliability): no collision. Reliability governs
  what one *call* does before a response is committed; this governs an answer
  that **was** committed.
* Unused, it costs nothing: an agent without the option mounts no branch, writes
  no state, and emits no event.

## When to reach for it

Reach for `'assist'` on any agent whose answers carry identifiers a human will
act on — port names, order numbers, account ids, serials — and read the events
for a week. Move to `'guard'` when the numbers say you should, and especially
when the model is a small one: naming the values back is the cheapest structural
help a weak model gets. Reach for `'rails'` only where an answer carrying an
invented identifier is worse than no answer at all.
